description_ru: Старая женщина отказывается продавать свой сад застройщику, но у неё на уме нечто более коварное, чем отказ. Тихая, остроумная история о терпении и плодах.
text:
The developer arrived on a Tuesday, which Miss Winifred Larch regarded as the first of his offences. Tuesdays, in her considered view, were days for ironing and quiet resentments, not for strangers in cream-coloured suits standing among her quince trees with their hands in their pockets, appraising them as if they were livestock.

"Wonderful space," said the developer. His name was Mr. Roland Pike, and he had the kind of teeth that appear in advertisements for dental insurance. "Really wonderful. Four acres, I understand? Ripe for the right kind of vision." "They are quince trees," said Miss Larch. "Not a vision."

She was eighty-three, as thin and upright as a heron, and she had lived in the house at the end of Cobbler's Lane since the winter her father died, which was longer ago than most of the village had been alive. The orchard behind it was a tangle of sixty ancient trees, gnarled and leaning, each with a wrinkled, ironic look, as if it had seen a great deal and thought poorly of most of it. In October the whole place smelled of honey and old books. The fruit hung heavy and yellow, furred like a baby's cheek, and entirely inedible when raw.

Mr. Pike smiled his insurance smile. He explained, with the unhurried warmth of a man who has never been refused anything of consequence, that the village needed housing, that the planning committee was sympathetic, and that the price he proposed was, frankly, a little embarrassing in its generosity. He named a sum. The sum was large enough to be rude. He gestured vaguely at the sky, a movement which, in his long experience, was the polite overture to a bulldozer, and added that there would be a little green space, naturally, for the children, and perhaps a tasteful water feature shaped like a leaf. "I shall consider it," said Miss Larch.

He went away delighted, because he had been in the business long enough to know that the phrase "I shall consider it" is the first stage of surrender. He would have been less delighted had he known that Miss Larch, at that moment, was already considering something else altogether.

She did not mention the offer to anyone, not to the vicar, not to the grocer, and certainly not to the cat, who was known to gossip. She went about her week as usual: the post office on Wednesday, the library on Thursday, a long, withering stare at the vicar on Sunday. But on Friday she took a stepladder, a pair of secateurs, and a large basket, and began, with the patient absorption of a surgeon, to harvest.

Quinces are a stubborn fruit. They cannot be eaten from the tree; they must be coaxed, by long cooking, into a state of grace, and then they become something marvellous, ruby-red and fragrant, tasting of roses and pears and a faint, regretful memory of apples. Miss Larch knew this better than anyone alive. For forty years she had made quince jelly in her kitchen, in cauldrons the size of small bathtubs, and for forty years she had given it away at Christmas, in jam jars labelled in a spidery hand, to people who had never quite understood what they were being given.

Now she worked with grim industry. By the end of the week the kitchen was a steaming cathedral of sugar and fruit, and the windows ran with condensation like the cheeks of a mourner. By the end of the month there were four hundred jars, lined up in the pantry like a small, glittering army. She labelled them all. Each label read, in exquisite copperplate, "Larch Orchard Quince. Last Harvest."

The last two words were a masterstroke, and she knew it. The village, on receiving this news, reacted in the manner of a flock of startled geese. It turned out that nearly everyone had eaten the jelly for decades, that it had been present at births, funerals, and at least one memorable divorce, and that nobody had realised it was precious until it was threatened with extinction. A queue formed at the gate. The vicar, in a rare moment of unity with his parish, bought three dozen jars. Even the butcher came, a man whose entire diet consisted of sausages and grudges.

Word travelled. A food journalist arrived from the city, tasted the jelly on a cracker, and went quiet for a moment in the way of a man hearing a long-lost song. Her article, "The Last Orchard," appeared the following Sunday, and was shared by people who had never in their lives been to the countryside but who felt, nonetheless, that something sacred was about to be lost. A television crew followed, then a petition, then a very earnest young woman with a banner.

Mr. Pike watched all of this with the dawning, uncomfortable awareness of a chess player who has realised that the old lady across the board has been playing a different game entirely. The planning committee, sensitive to public opinion in the way that weathercocks are sensitive to wind, quietly withdrew its sympathy. The housing scheme was reclassified as "under review", a phrase which, in the language of local government, means "buried at sea".

He came to see her one last time, in December, in a grey mood and a crumpled coat. Miss Larch received him in the kitchen, where the last of the jars stood in ranks, and offered him tea. "You planned this," he said.

"I made jelly," said Miss Larch. "People are surprisingly attached to what they have already put on their toast." He looked at her for a long moment, and then, to his own surprise, he laughed. "May I buy a jar?"

"They are all sold," she said. "But I shall put one by for you. In the spring, when the blossom comes, you must visit. Quince blossom is rather a fine thing. Nobody ever thinks of it as a vision."

And, much later, when the old woman was gone and the orchard had passed to the village in trust, Mr. Pike was seen on a bench among the trees each October, eating, with a dreamy and unprofitable expression, a slice of toast.

questions.question: Who was Mr. Roland Pike?
questions.answer: A developer who wanted to buy the orchard.

questions.question: What did Miss Larch do with the quinces?
questions.answer: She made hundreds of jars of quince jelly labelled Last Harvest.

questions.question: Why did the planning committee withdraw its support?
questions.answer: Public opinion turned against the scheme after the news spread.

questions.question: What happened to the orchard in the end?
questions.answer: It passed to the village in trust.
